items.title: 13.8.2 Reaction of silver halides (AgX) with aqueous ammonia

blocks.text: Adding aqueous ammonia tests the solubility of the silver halide precipitates. AgF is soluble in water and gives no precipitate, so ammonia has no effect. The white precipitate of silver chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia to give a colourless solution of the diamminesilver(I) complex: AgCl(s) + 2NH3(aq) gives [Ag(NH3)2]+(aq) + Cl-(aq). The cream precipitate of silver bromide dissolves in concentrated ammonia, also giving a colourless solution: AgBr(s) + 2NH3(aq) gives [Ag(NH3)2]+ + Br-. The yellow precipitate of silver iodide does not dissolve in dilute or concentrated ammonia, so there is no change. Table 13.6 summarises the sequence.

blocks.caption: Action of Ag+ followed by ammonia on halides (Table 13.6)

blocks.prompt: Write the equations for KI with Ag+ followed by NH3 and state what is observed; and explain the different solubilities of the silver halides in ammonia (Quick Check 13.4b, c).
blocks.explanation: KI(aq) + AgNO3(aq) gives AgI(s) + KNO3(aq): a pale yellow precipitate. On adding ammonia, dilute or concentrated, nothing changes; the yellow solid remains. Ammonia dissolves a silver halide by forming the [Ag(NH3)2]+ complex, which competes with the lattice: AgCl is the most soluble of the three, so dilute ammonia suffices; AgBr is less soluble and needs concentrated ammonia; AgI is so insoluble that the complex cannot pull enough Ag+ into solution.

items: AgCl dissolves in dilute NH3, AgBr only in concentrated NH3 (both give colourless [Ag(NH3)2]+), AgI dissolves in neither; AgF never precipitates. Table 13.6 gives the systematic sequence.
